kinds.d: Fossil wood replaced by silica or other minerals, rough, slab or polished.

x.d: Late Triassic logs (about 225–207 million years ago) of the Chinle Formation, mostly Araucarioxylon arizonicum; removal from Petrified Forest National Park is prohibited.
Silicified wood from the north-west coast of Madagascar.
Silicified wood from Banten and Mount Halimun Salak National Park area.
Trunks over 3 m in diameter in the Sarmiento and Jaramillo Petrified Forests, Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
Wood replaced by opal, notably Chinchilla Red from Chinchilla, Queensland.

kinds.d: Fossil leaf, fern, frond, seed or cone, as an impression, compression or nodule. Petrified wood is separate.

x.d: Fern and seed-fern fronds such as Pecopteris preserved in siderite concretions about 309 million years old from Illinois; the flora has over 400 species.

v.d: Tullimonstrum gregarium, Illinois state fossil, known only from Mazon Creek

x.dt: split ironstone nodules · permit needed at Braidwood State Fish and Wildlife Area

x.d: Permian seed-plant genus of Gondwana with tongue-shaped leaves 2–30 cm long; matching fossils across southern continents supported continental drift.
x.dt: leaf impressions · India, Australia, South America, Africa, Antarctica

x.d: Leaf fossils of Ginkgo, a living fossil whose genus first appears in the Middle Jurassic; localities include Scarborough (Jurassic) and McAbee, British Columbia (Eocene).
Fossil palm, fern and sycamore leaves of the Eocene Green River Formation, some showing insect damage.

kinds.d: Layered fossil structure built by microbial mats, rough or polished.

x.d: About 3.4 billion-year-old stromatolites in the Strelley Pool chert of the Pilbara Craton, Western Australia.
Living stromatolites at Hamelin Pool, Western Australia (protected, not collectable); the modern analogue for fossils.

kinds.d: Fossil track, footprint, burrow, boring or coprolite left by an organism rather than its body.

x.d: Fossil track of a walking dinosaur; a trackway is a sequence of tracks from a single animal. Famous sites include Lark Quarry, the Paluxy River and Ardley.

v.n: Paluxy River, Dinosaur Valley State Park

v.d: Oxfordshire; most survive only as replicas

x.d: Fossilised droppings, named by William Buckland in 1829; mined for phosphate in nineteenth-century eastern England.

v.d: Found by Mary Anning in ichthyosaur skeletons

x.d: Stomach or gizzard stone; real gastroliths are rounded, polished on high points and differ from local rock.
Burrows such as vertical Skolithos tubes and branching Thalassinoides systems, and borings in hard surfaces.

notes: Bolivian and Australian stromatolite sales, Madagascar petrified wood specifics and polished-slab details not confirmed by pages, so left generic.
